Eggs of the Southern royal albatross (Diomedea epomophora) are incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime maintained consistently by both parents during the incubation period. Under these conditions, hatching occurs after approximately 79 days [ab = approximately 79 days], an extended developmental duration that is typical among large procellariiform seabirds and reflects the substantial yolk reserves required to sustain embryonic growth at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a wet weight of 500 grams [Wwb = 500 grams], a relatively modest mass compared to the ultimate adult body size they will achieve. This neonatal mass is supported entirely by endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatch, after which parental provisioning begins in earnest. The thermal environment of the nest, remaining near 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] during brooding, drives rapid growth, and the chick enters a prolonged nestling phase characterized by steady mass gain and feather development. Field measurements indicate that the entire incubation cycle is tightly synchronized with the austral summer, ensuring that hatching coincides with peak marine productivity in the subantarctic waters surrounding the breeding colonies.

Under the sustained metabolic conditions typical of an actively growing nestling at approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], fledging occurs at an age of approximately 204 days after hatching [tx = approximately 204 days after hatching]. This post-hatching developmental period, exceeding eight months, is among the longest recorded for any albatross species and reflects the substantial time required to attain both flight feather maturation and sufficient body mass for independent foraging. The chicks reach an ultimate wet weight prior to fledging of approximately 17,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 17,000 grams], though this asymptotic mass is not maintained in adult life; after fledging and the loss of residual body water and fat stores, mean adult weight stabilizes around 8.5 kilograms. Males of the species are typically 2 to 3 kilograms heavier than females, a sexual size dimorphism that becomes apparent during the later stages of the nestling period. The extended fledging interval is energetically demanding on the parents, who alternate between foraging trips lasting days and brief visits to provision the chick with regurgitated oil and partially digested prey. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Diomedea exulans show similar developmental timelines, confirming the conserved life-history strategy of slow growth and delayed independence among the great albatrosses.

Sexual maturation in Diomedea epomophora follows an extended juvenile period, with individuals reaching puberty at an age of 612 days after hatching [tp = 612 days after hatching] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of gonadal maturity is somewhat misleading, however, because first successful breeding does not occur for many more years due to the species' complex social structure and the need to acquire a breeding territory. The onset of puberty at 612 days marks the initiation of gametogenesis, but behavioral maturity—including the ability to attract a mate and successfully incubate an egg–requires additional experience and physical conditioning. Young birds typically return to natal colonies at around three to four years of age, engaging in courtship displays and pair formation before attempting their first reproductive event. The physiological state at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] during the active metabolic periods of these juveniles supports rapid development of the reproductive organs. Field observations suggest that the interval between achieving puberty and actually breeding varies considerably among individuals, influenced by food availability and the density of competing adults in the colony. This protracted maturation contrasts sharply with smaller procellariiform species, which often breed within their first two years.

The age at first successful reproduction for the Southern royal albatross is a remarkably delayed 9 years after hatching [tR = 9 years after hatching], reflecting one of the longest pre-breeding periods among all seabirds at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This deferred investment in reproduction is a classic K-selected life-history strategy, optimizing adult survival at the expense of early reproductive output. Under the thermal regime of approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic period of breeding adults, the species produces a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and raises only one clutch every two years [F_R_i = only one clutch every two years]. This extremely low fecundity is balanced by exceptionally high adult and juvenile survival probabilities, demographic parameters that have been confirmed through long-term banding studies on the Otago Peninsula and the subantarctic islands. The first breeding attempt often fails, but experienced pairs achieve high hatching and fledging success.

Maximum lifespan in this species is estimated at 58 years [am = 58 years], a longevity that places Diomedea epomophora among the longest-lived of all wild birds at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, sustained at a body temperature near 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], is accompanied by negligible reproductive senescence; individuals continue to breed successfully well into their fifth decade. The extended lifespan compensates for the extremely low maximum reproductive rate, as a single female may produce only 25 to 30 chicks over a lifetime of breeding attempts. Given that a maximum reproductive rate of one egg per two years is the biological reality for this species, population persistence depends critically on the survival of both adults and the few offspring they produce. The demographics of this species are therefore highly sensitive to anthropogenic threats such as longline fishing, which disproportionately affects older, reproductively valuable individuals. Conservation efforts focus on reducing bycatch mortality and protecting nesting habitat to ensure that the rare reproductive events that do occur have the highest possible probability of success. Comparative analyses with other Diomedea species confirm that the combination of delayed maturity, low fecundity, and extreme longevity is a conserved strategy within the genus.
